hints: Look at the very top of the cells in Fig. 8.1 in region Y - these are tiny finger-like folds of cell surface membrane that increase surface area for detecting chemicals.
walkthrough:
Spot the Finger-Like Folds**
You are looking at the tip of the chemoreceptor cell that sticks out into the mouth cavity. The membrane is not flat, it is folded into many tiny projections. This is the classic way cells increase surface area to catch more stimulus molecules.

Name the Structure**
Those projections are microvilli, collectively called the brush border. More membrane here means more $Na^+$ channels and receptor proteins in contact with dissolved salt.

hints: Think about what would happen if dissolved chemicals in saliva could leak down the gaps between the cells instead of having to go through the top membrane at Y.
walkthrough:
What Tight Junctions Do**
Tight-junction proteins link neighbouring cells and seal the space between them, restricting and regulating movement between cells. The membranes do not fuse into one continuous membrane.

Why That Matters Here**
The stimulus chemicals must only enter via the exposed top membrane at Y so the correct cell detects them. Sealing stops ions and other substances leaking down the sides and stimulating the wrong part of the cell or reaching tissue fluid below.
Final answer: prevent movement / leakage of chemicals / ions / substances between the chemoreceptor cells.

walkthrough:
$Na^+$ Entry Creates a Receptor Potential in Cell A**
Dissolved salt provides $Na^+$ ions that enter chemoreceptor cell A through channel proteins in the microvilli at Y. Influx of positive ions makes the inside less negative, so the cell surface membrane is depolarised. This graded depolarisation is a receptor potential. If it reaches threshold, the signal continues.

Calcium Links Electricity to Secretion**
Depolarisation spreads to the base of cell A and opens voltage-gated $Ca^{2+}$ channels. $Ca^{2+}$ ions enter the cytoplasm. Calcium is the universal trigger for secretion, so do not confuse it with $Na^+$. $Na^+$ starts the receptor potential, $Ca^{2+}$ starts transmitter release.

Exocytosis of Neurotransmitter**
$Ca^{2+}$ causes vesicles containing neurotransmitter to move to and fuse with the presynaptic membrane at the base of cell A. Neurotransmitter is released by exocytosis into the tiny gap next to sensory neurone B. This converts the electrical signal in the receptor cell into a chemical signal.

Depolarisation and Action Potential in Neurone B**
Neurotransmitter diffuses across and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane of sensory neurone B. This opens $Na^+$ channels in B, $Na^+$ enter and depolarise B. If threshold is reached, voltage-gated channels open and an action potential is generated in sensory neurone B to carry the taste signal to the brain.

Final answer: $Na^+$ enter cell A through channels in microvilli / Y; membrane depolarised forming receptor potential, reaching threshold; voltage-gated $Ca^{2+}$ channels open, $Ca^{2+}$ enter cell A; vesicles fuse with presynaptic membrane releasing neurotransmitter by exocytosis; neurotransmitter binds receptors on neurone B; $Na^+$ channels open in B, $Na^+$ enter, depolarising it to threshold to trigger action potential.
